findings.section: 3-do.md (whole file); also 4-say.md; 1-fast.md Look first; 2-deep.md Try it callouts
findings.evidence: Rule TOOLS-items.md sync: 'Only items with status: ready are printed ... A file with no item still gets its H1 and the line Nothing here yet.' All 3 tasks (data/22-ebs/tasks.json), all 4 speak items (speak.json) and all 32 cards (cards.json) have status 'candidate'. So 3-do.md and 4-say.md are empty. The Look first region in 1-fast.md (task:start id=ebs-t01) is empty. The two 'Try it ... See 3-do.md' callouts in 2-deep.md (Elastic Volumes, restored volume) point to an empty page. TOOLS-rules.md R5: 'A reviewer sets cards, speak items and tasks to ready in the stage of that kind, after the item lint is clean.' The reader is promised a task and spoken answers and gets none. Fix: set-status ready for ebs-t01..t03, ebs-s01..s04 and the cards after their item lint is clean, then sync 22.

findings.section: Instance store data lives on the host and ends with the instance (3 min)
findings.quote: ### Instance store data lives on the host and ends with the instance (3 min)
findings.evidence: READER.md: 'Headings, tables and captions must give a correct gist on their own.' From the heading alone, 'ends with the instance' reads as 'ends at termination', which is the exact wrong belief of Predict 2. The data also ends at a stop: instance-store-data-erased-on-stop ('data on any instance store volumes is erased'). Suggested heading: 'Instance store data lives on the host and ends at a stop or termination'.
findings.resolution: fix-22: the heading text is fixed by brief.json (TOOLS-rules R4, L905) and is the anchor of question Review links; a change needs the orchestrator to change the brief. The body now makes the stop explicit (step 4 and the Stop-and-answer).

findings.section: Instance store ...; Recycle Bin and snapshot lock ...; Each snapshot stores changed blocks ...
findings.quote: 3. **Lose it after a stop.** ... / 2. **Write a rule in each Region.** ... / **Figure.** Deleting an older snapshot keeps the blocks that newer snapshots still use
findings.evidence: STYLE.md line 76: 'Stop and answer applies the text to a new case ... Never ask for a sentence she can copy from the paragraph above.' Three Stop-and-answer items are answered by a bold step label or a figure caption a few lines above: the nightly-stop cache question ('Lose it after a stop.'), the Recycle Bin rule in US West question ('Write a rule in each Region.'), and the 'bill barely drops' question (figure caption). A skim gives the answer. Change each to a case that needs the mechanism, for example a reboot plus a stop in one scenario, a rule with a tag filter that does not match, or a snapshot whose blocks were all overwritten later.
findings.resolution: fix-22: three Stop-and-answer items rewritten: reboot then stop; snapshot whose blocks were all rewritten; governance lock plus a Recycle Bin rule in another Region.

findings.section: SSD volumes serve small random IO and HDD volumes serve large sequential reads (4 min)
findings.quote: Why do small random reads fail on HDD? There, an I/O of [1 MiB or less counts as a 1 MiB I/O credit](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-hdd-io-counted-as-1-mib).
findings.evidence: STYLE.md line 215: the reason is what she tells a customer. The sentence gives the rule but not the effect. The step she has to infer is that a small read uses up a whole 1 MiB of the throughput budget, while sequential I/Os are merged. Fact ebs-hdd-io-counted-as-1-mib quote: 'an I/O request of 1 MiB or less counts as a 1 MiB I/O credit. However, if the I/Os are sequential, they are merged into 1 MiB I/O blocks and count only as a 1 MiB I/O credit.' Add one cause-and-effect sentence, such as 'so a 16 KiB random read costs as much as a 1 MiB read, and sequential reads are merged and cost one credit'. Also 'fail' is too strong: 'perform badly'.
findings.resolution: fix-22: cause and effect added; 'perform badly' wording.

findings.section: io2 Block Express buys more IOPS lower latency and higher durability (4 min)
findings.quote: Why pay more? It runs on the [next generation of Amazon EBS storage server architecture](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-block-express-definition).
findings.evidence: A product label, not a reason (STYLE.md line 215). The same fact holds the real cause, which also explains the Nitro-only limits she must remember. ebs-faq-block-express-definition quote: 'Block Express does this by using Scalable Reliable Datagrams (SRD), a high-performance lower-latency network protocol, to communicate with Nitro System-based EC2 instances.' Suggested reason: 'Block Express talks to Nitro instances over a faster network protocol, so the full IOPS and the lowest latency need a Nitro instance.'
findings.resolution: fix-22: reason now Scalable Reliable Datagrams (SRD) to Nitro instances (ebs-faq-block-express-definition).

findings.section: The instance and its EBS bandwidth can cap a fast volume (4 min)
findings.quote: Why does the instance matter? Every I/O leaves it, and EBS is a [multi-tenant block storage service](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-multi-tenant-rate-limiting) that uses [rate limiting](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-faq-multi-tenant-rate-limiting).
findings.evidence: The reason given does not explain the claim. Fact ebs-faq-multi-tenant-rate-limiting quote: 'EBS is a multi-tenant block storage service. We employ rate limiting as a mechanism to avoid resource contention.' That is the volume side, which keeps one volume within its provisioned performance. The instance cap comes from the instance's own path to EBS (ebs-optimized-dedicated-bandwidth: 'dedicated bandwidth for Amazon EBS I/O'), which each instance type sizes differently. Suggested reason: 'Every I/O travels over the instance's own link to EBS, and each instance type has a fixed size for that link.'

findings.section: Each snapshot stores changed blocks but can restore the whole volume (4 min)
findings.quote: 3. **Mind the cache.** A snapshot [does not include data that has been cached](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-excludes-cached-data) by the application.
findings.evidence: The step names a risk but says neither what goes wrong nor what to do, and it drops half of the source. ebs-snapshot-excludes-cached-data quote: 'The snapshot includes only the data that was written to the volume at the time the snapshot was requested. It does not include data that has been cached by applications or the operating system.' Say what this means for her: a snapshot of a busy database can miss recent writes that are still in memory, so the writes are flushed or paused before the snapshot. The Say it line 'The thing to watch is cached data' then gives a customer something to act on.
findings.resolution: fix-22: the step names application and operating system caches and says to pause writes first (ebs-snapshot-consistency-pause-writes-or-unmount).

findings.section: Recycle Bin and snapshot lock stop snapshots from being deleted too early (3 min)
findings.quote: 4. **Use compliance mode against everyone.** In compliance mode, after the cooling-off period, [you must wait for the lock to expire](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-lock-compliance-mode).
findings.evidence: 'cooling-off period' is used here and in the key of quiz Question 16 ('without a cooling-off period') but never explained. A verified fact exists: ebs-snapshot-lock-cooling-off-range (claim: 'The optional cooling-off period for a compliance-mode snapshot lock can range from 1 to 72 hours; omit it to lock in compliance mode immediately'). Add one sentence: during the optional cooling-off period, users with permission can still unlock; without one, the lock is final at once.

findings.section: Look first (3 min); 2-deep.md Copying or sharing a snapshot (table)
findings.quote: read three **Region** settings: encryption by default, its key, and **block public access** for snapshots
findings.evidence: Block public access for snapshots appears in Look first and in the sharing table ('Yes, unless block public access is on') but is never explained in 1-fast.md or 2-deep.md. Task ebs-t01 then expects the reader to read the values block-all-sharing, block-new-sharing or unblocked. Facts exist (ebs-snapshot-bpa-two-modes, ebs-snapshot-bpa-regional-account-setting, both used by ebs-t01). Add one sentence in the sharing subsection: a Region setting that stops snapshots from being shared publicly.
findings.resolution: fix-22: sharing step 4 explains block public access for snapshots (Regional setting that blocks public sharing).

findings.section: Choose it or not: gp3 or io2 Block Express or an HDD type; Signals and traps; 2-deep.md io2 and Multi-Attach subsections
findings.quote: Provisioned IOPS [up to 256,000](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-io2-max-iops-ratio) on Nitro-based instances
findings.evidence: 'Nitro' decides several answers (the 256,000 or 32,000 IOPS limit, Multi-Attach to 16 Nitro instances, the stems of Questions 3, 14 and 15). It is never defined in chapter 22 or in chapter 16 (no match for 'nitro' in 16-ec2/1-fast.md or 2-deep.md), and data/terms.json has no entry. STYLE.md: spell out and explain each term at first use. Add a one-line plain meaning, for example 'the current AWS hardware and hypervisor platform that most current instance types run on', grounded in a fact, or link to where the book defines it.
findings.resolution: fix-22: io2 step 2 defines Nitro with ec2-nitro-system-definition.

findings.section: Copying or sharing a snapshot puts the backup in another Region or account (3 min)
findings.quote: Only snapshots [encrypted with a customer managed key](../facts/ebs.md#ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable) can be shared.
findings.evidence: Read alone, the sentence says no unencrypted snapshot can be shared. The table a few lines above says the opposite ('Unencrypted | Yes | Yes, unless block public access is on'). The source limits the rule to encrypted snapshots. ebs-snapshot-aws-managed-key-not-shareable quote: 'You can't share snapshots that are encrypted with the default AWS managed key. You can only share snapshots that are encrypted with a customer managed key.' Rewrite: 'Of encrypted snapshots, only those encrypted with a customer managed key can be shared.'

findings.quote: **FAQ 4.** Can you stop paying for provisioned IOPS by detaching the volume? ... No. > "Yes, you will be billed for the IOPS provisioned when it is disconnected from an instance."
findings.evidence: The answer 'No.' is followed straight away by a quote that starts with 'Yes'. A reader who skims, in her second language, sees both words and can keep the wrong one. Reword the question so that it matches the quote: 'Are you still billed for provisioned IOPS after you detach the volume?' with the answer 'Yes.'

findings.quote: **Requirement.** The database must lose at most 24 hours of data, recover within 8 hours and survive a full volume. Which solution is the fastest to implement? ... **Decision.** A separate encrypted gp3 data volume for the database, with daily snapshots ... A larger volume is no backup
findings.evidence: The decision rejects only one of the three options, and only on the backup point. It never says why a separate data volume meets 'survive a full volume' (temporary files can no longer fill the database volume), why a daily snapshot meets the 24-hour data-loss limit and the 8-hour recovery target (restore a volume from the newest snapshot), or why the managed database is not chosen now ('fastest to implement'; STARTUP.md line 438 'Accepts: one instance in one Availability Zone until chapter 26'). The section also lists the same three facts three times (fast Startup example, figure caption, numbered list 1 to 3) and is over its budget (lint W201: 334 words, limit 280). Replace the repetition with one sentence for each rejected option.
findings.resolution: fix-22: partly fixed: the decision now says why (temporary files can no longer fill it, a daily snapshot limits loss to one day, a managed database takes longer). The figure steps stay: L703 requires them to equal the diagram spec. W201 stays a warning.

findings.section: ebs-s01 (prompt 'If that instance fails tomorrow, what do we lose, and how long are we offline?')
findings.quote: "ten_second": "If only the instance fails, the database volume survives and we attach it again. If the whole zone fails, we restore last night's snapshot."
findings.evidence: Ana asks two things, what is lost and how long Callvale is offline. Neither the 10-second nor the 60-second answer gives a time. Both end at data loss ('a zone failure costs at most one day of new data'). The story target is RTO 8 hours (STARTUP.md line 94: 'Stage 1 targets: RPO 24 hours, RTO 8 hours'). Add one spoken sentence, for example 'Rebuilding takes a few hours: a new instance, a volume from the snapshot, and a slow first hour while the blocks load. Our target is under eight hours.' The time values must be story values, not AWS facts.

findings.quote: An EBS volume is a durable, block-level storage device that can persist independently from the running life of instances.
findings.evidence: READER.md: she 'struggles to articulate clearly when nervous' and needs a one-breath definition she can say. 'persist independently from the running life of instances' is document wording that is hard to say. Keep the fact links, but put the spoken Say it in simpler words, for example 'a network disk for one instance, in one zone, that keeps its data when the instance stops'. The fact-linked AWS wording can stay on the line below.
findings.resolution: fix-22: the Say it keeps the fact-linked AWS definition; the plain spoken version is in 4-say.md (ebs-s01 now published), and 1-fast is near its word limit.

findings.section: io2 Block Express buys more IOPS lower latency and higher durability; EBS encryption covers the volume its snapshots and the path to the instance
findings.quote: ### EBS encryption covers the volume its snapshots and the path to the instance (4 min)
findings.evidence: Without commas, list headings read as one noun phrase ('the volume its snapshots', 'more IOPS lower latency'). In her second language this blocks the gist. If the heading slug rule forbids commas, reword to avoid a list, for example 'EBS encryption protects the volume, ...' -> 'Encryption on the host protects the volume and every snapshot of it'.
findings.resolution: fix-22: heading texts are fixed by brief.json (R4, L905) and anchor question Review links; a change needs a brief change by the orchestrator.

findings.quote: "answer": "Not per volume. Once encryption by default is enabled for a Region, you cannot disable it for individual volumes or snapshots in that Region. Each Region needs its own setting."
findings.evidence: 'Not per volume.' is a fragment that a listener cannot follow. The question is yes or no ('can someone still create an unencrypted volume?'). Start with the answer: 'No, not in that Region. Once encryption by default is on, ...'.
findings.resolution: fix-22: the answer starts 'No, not for one volume.'
